description: We’re a two-person team from Bolivia building Lunar Window, a web tool for comparing landing sites near the Moon’s south pole. Using NASA/JPL data, we’ll show when the Sun and Earth are visible from each site and find windows when both are visible at the same time. This helps users compare locations and dates for solar power and direct communication with Earth.
summary: We built LUNAR ORACLE to answer a practical question: if we want to reach the Moon on a given date, where should we look for a landing site, and what could make that mission fail? Our web app compares 12,892 sectors across the lunar south pole using NASA LOLA terrain and JPL ephemerides. A 3D map shows candidate, constrained and unresolved areas, while a timeline reveals changes in sunlight and Earth visibility. Users can then examine battery reserves, thermal conditions, communication opportunities and higher-resolution terrain where data are available. If a scenario does not meet its requirements, the system explores changes to timing, location or activities without quietly lowering those requirements. Gemini helps interpret requests and explain calculated results; the scientific engine performs the calculations. We want to make early mission trade-offs understandable and traceable for students, educators and mission-planning research.
details:
We are Rudy Gabriel Chambi Chambi and Ramiro Ariel Quenta Ramos, from Project Ukanakax chhullunkhayat luratawa. We built LUNAR ORACLE for the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge because choosing where to land also means understanding when to arrive, how to stay powered and how to communicate.

A user starts with a mission request in everyday language. The application turns dates, stay duration and requirements into a scenario and compares 12,892 regional sectors between 80 and 90 degrees south. An interactive 3D map and a shared timeline show terrain, sunlight and Earth visibility. Green identifies candidates under the selected model, yellow indicates limited margin, red indicates failed criteria and grey preserves unresolved areas.

Our main innovation is connecting site selection to the consequences of that decision. The mission study evaluates battery charge, solar production, consumption, reserves, heating and thermal conditions. A conditional radio budget combines lunar visibility with contact geometry for representative Deep Space Network antennas in Goldstone, Madrid and Canberra. Users can investigate delays, reduced solar production or communication outages and compare changes to dates, destinations and activities. The searches preserve the stated requirements and explain when no examined alternative meets them.

We also developed terrain-based rover planning. The system searches routes across the native local terrain, considers slope and footprint classifications, estimates rolling, climbing and auxiliary energy, and calculates the return journey while preserving a declared reserve. This helps users investigate how far a rover could explore under the model’s assumptions. Subpixel rocks, wheel–soil interaction and actual hardware performance remain outside the validated scope.

For detailed destination studies, we evaluate a declared landing-dispersion ellipse, local slopes and roughness, and separate terrain horizons for panel and antenna heights. NASA LOLA data with 80 m grid spacing support the regional analysis; 5 m products are used only inside their actual Site01 and Site04 coverage.

Additional capabilities include outbound and return orbital boundary calculations using Earth, Moon and Sun gravity with NASA/JPL ephemerides. Users can import hardware profiles and telemetry records with provenance and initialize model states from compatible observations. These capabilities establish a foundation for a future digital twin; the current prototype is not connected to a physical spacecraft.

We built the interface with React, TypeScript and Three.js/React Three Fiber, and the scientific backend with Python, FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, Rasterio, PyProj and SpiceyPy. Gemini helps structure requests and explain computed evidence. A deterministic interpreter supports compatible requests when the AI service is unavailable.

The implementation passed 383 Python tests and 225 JavaScript tests. A separate SPICE calculation cross-checks Horizons geometry, and exported reports retain inputs, assumptions, source records and terrain/kernel hashes. Our goal is to make early mission trade-offs understandable, reproducible and accessible. Hardware calibration, authenticated telemetry and independent physical validation remain necessary before operational use.
